extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, judges, legal scholars, and readers interested in administrative law and Supreme Court doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion-piece assessing the modern administrative state and recent Supreme Court cases (e.g., Chevron, Jarkesy, CFPB), arguing for a realistic, historically informed recalibration of judicial deference and procedural modernization. It discusses why past precedents may not fit today's agency landscape and what factors courts should weigh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate agencies against the Constitution’s original meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: This questioning has been phrased mainly in terms of our constitutional founding, and rightly so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing agency power or structural questions (e.g., independence from the president), courts should consider the Constitution’s original meaning as a primary datum. The piece cites Justices’ reliance on originalist arguments in recent cases (e.g., CFPB funding issue) as an appropriate starting point for constitutional appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for modern administrative impact and historical distance from precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: “Atlas Roofing is 50 years old… the government is much more likely to affect you and proceed against you before one of its own agencies than in court, and that concern and that threat is far greater today than when Atlas Roofing was set up.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should weigh how much the administrative state has grown since older precedents; a precedent established in a very different administrative era may not fit today’s realities. Consider both how much agencies now affect daily life and whether the factual context of a precedent remains comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use realism (practical realities) alongside originalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrative state's doubters are not just originalists; they’re realists, too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial assessment should incorporate pragmatic facts about agency behavior, capacities, and effects, not only abstract originalist theory. Real-world institutional functioning — e.g., how agencies operate day-to-day and how they affect regulated parties — is a relevant input into doctrinal decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reassess Chevron deference in light of changed institutional conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron... directed lower courts to give agencies great leeway in administering broadly worded statutes... In hindsight, it fell far short in all of these objectives, and may well have undermined them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding whether to reaffirm, modify, or overrule Chevron, courts should evaluate whether Chevron still (a) elevates expertise, (b) preserves political accountability in presidential administration, (c) simplifies judicial review, and (d) reinforces Congress’s legislative centrality. If Chevron no longer serves these goals because agencies have evolved, recalibration is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor a prudential, measured re-balancing over wholesale renunciation or blind reaffirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: This does not necessarily mean a complete renunciation of courts giving some weight to an agency’s interpretation of vague statutes... But it does counsel against simply reaffirming Chevron in a vastly different era of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should seek a middle path: preserve sensible kinds of deference where justified (e.g., genuine expertise, accountability structures) while curbing deference where institutional changes make it unwise. Avoid reflexive all-or-nothing doctrinal moves; evaluate types of cases and statutory contexts individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider specific agency practices as evidence for doctrinal change
rubrics_metrics.description: They are far more willing and able to leverage regulatory uncertainty under vague statutes. They are more creative in imposing new policies outside of the Administrative Procedure Act’s notice-and-comment procedures. They are more adept at colluding with state or foreign regulators to whipsaw U.S. companies...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether agencies are (a) exploiting statutory ambiguity to expand power, (b) bypassing APA notice-and-comment, or (c) coordinating with other jurisdictions in ways that amplify regulatory reach. Such behaviors are relevant facts weighing against broad deference and support stricter judicial scrutiny or limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess institutional design features and their historical novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: When the solicitor general vaguely invoked 'history' to support the CFPB’s power, Alito took a careful look at that history and pressed her to concede that the agency’s particular combination of fiscal independence and regulatory power was actually unprecedented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should examine whether structural features (e.g., independent funding, insulation from presidential control) are historically rooted or novel. Novel combinations that concentrate power without historical analogue may justify heightened constitutional or statutory scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reevaluate older precedents (e.g., 1935 independent-agency precedents) given modern agency activism
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1935 precedent affirming the constitutionality of 'independent' agencies... might have made practical sense (though much less constitutional sense) in its own time... It makes much less sense today, when a turbocharged FTC, SEC, and FCC are profoundly more activist, political, and ambitious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedents should be revisited when the institutional facts that supported them have materially changed. Courts should ask whether past practical justifications still hold and whether continued adherence undermines constitutional structure today.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modernize judicial procedures for case-taking, decisions, and interim emergency relief
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be unrealistic for the Court not to think hard about modernizing its own procedures for taking cases, issuing decisions, and granting emergency relief... developments during and after the Covid-19 emergency suggest that the justices already are undertaking that procedural reconsideration—carefully, prudently, and realistically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond doctrinal change, courts should reform procedural rules (e.g., certiorari standards, sequencing, standards for nationwide injunctions and emergency stays) to better cope with rapid regulatory action and to avoid ad hoc nationwide policies from lower-court injunctions. Procedural modernization should be careful and pragmatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance constitutional logic with administrative experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. famously asserted that 'the life of the law is not logic but experience.' Actually, the law needs both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal decisionmaking should integrate principled constitutional analysis with empirical and institutional understanding of how agencies operate. Doctrinal choices should be informed by both normative legal theory and the practical consequences of agency behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider whether agencies have supplanted Congress as the policy center
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies have fully supplanted Congress as the center of gravity for American policymaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An evaluation of agency deference should consider the separation-of-powers implications of agencies effectively making policy that Congress traditionally would make. If agencies functionally displace Congress, courts should account for that when calibrating deference and enforcing statutory limits.
